article.name: Hivemind (Activeloop)
article.summary: Hivemind is a multi-agent memory and trace-sharing system built around Activeloop Deeplake workspaces. It captures structured agent events, creates session summaries, mines reusable skills, and exposes the data through a virtual filesystem and retrieval hooks. This assessment describes pinned public source and documentation; it does not establish runtime quality or isolation.

contact.note: The official pinned README publishes hello@activeloop.ai as a contact for teams running coding agents. No commit/profile metadata, third-party directory, or inferred address was used.

who_what.text: The official README identifies Activeloop as the builder and presents Hivemind as shared memory for coding agents; the architecture guide shows a TypeScript core with adapters for several agent harnesses.
The central backend is a Deeplake org/workspace accessed through an API client; local hooks, CLI commands, virtual-filesystem handling and workers implement capture, reads and derived artifacts.

architecture.text: The Deeplake `sessions` table stores one JSONB event per row with stable id, session path, filename, author, project, agent, plugin version, size and timestamps; `message_embedding` is nullable. The `memory` table stores generated text summaries with optional 768-dimensional embeddings and similar author/project/agent metadata.

Capture hooks serialize prompt, tool-call, tool-result and assistant-turn data, redact secret-like values, optionally embed the event locally, then write an idempotent row keyed by event id. The summary worker writes a separate AI-generated summary, so raw events and summaries have distinct update and deletion paths.

A third `skills` table stores a versioned skill body with project/project key, local path, install target, source session ids, source agent, scope, author, contributors, version and timestamps. Workers mine recent sessions and install or share `SKILL.md` files; Hivemind also includes separate rules, goals, docs and code-graph features.

behavior.text: Capture is enabled by default for supported integrations and can be disabled globally or for a directory tree. Captured event rows are append-like, use stable ids to avoid duplicates on retry, and can carry an embedding; periodic or session-end workers derive summaries and skills from the captured events.

Session pruning deletes the selected author's raw event rows for each session path and deletes the corresponding summary row. Skill edits generally insert a new version and readers choose the latest version; the SkillOpt publish path also writes a new team-scoped version directly. These paths do not establish erasure of backups or every local copy.

The virtual filesystem exposes memory and session records as files, while grep retrieval searches the summary and raw-session tables together. With a query embedding it unions semantic and lexical candidates, ranks by score, de-duplicates by path and caps each branch; without an embedding it falls back to lexical matching. The code can flag a result set as truncated when caps are reached.

Code-document search is a separate retrieval path and adds an active-status plus project-key filter, retaining legacy rows whose project field is empty. The ordinary memory/session search does not add an equivalent project or author predicate in the inspected SQL; it uses the path filter and the authenticated org/workspace selected for the request.

metrics.evidence: Search and result formatting code were inspected; no benchmark questions were run or scored.
Summary replacement, session append, and skill versioning paths were inspected; no correction or staleness probes were run.
Session-prune hard-delete code was inspected; no post-delete reads or backup-retention checks were run.
Workspace routing, API identity and search predicates were inspected; no cross-user, cross-workspace or cross-project workload was executed.
Stored event and skill provenance fields were inspected; no retrieved claim was adjudicated against source text.
No runtime timings or consistency probes were collected.
No model-token or cost measurements were collected for this review; README figures are upstream-reported and not reproduced.
Schemas and optional embeddings were inspected; no stored-size or storage-efficiency measurements were collected.

limits.text: The README describes workspace-level sharing: users in a workspace can read its captured data. Per-directory routing can select another org/workspace for both reads and writes, or disable capture; this review did not test authorization or cross-workspace isolation.

The inspected memory/session search SQL filters by path but not by author or project. A caller may therefore retrieve other workspace members' traces unless the workspace boundary or a higher layer constrains access; code-document search has its own project filter.

Session prune removes raw rows and the matching generated summary for a session. The reviewed path does not demonstrate deletion from backups, caches, exported traces, or copies already pulled to local skill directories.

Generated summaries and skills are model-produced artifacts. Provenance fields identify authors, source sessions, agents and versions, but the inspected retrieval path does not adjudicate whether a generated claim is supported by its source events.

The published LoCoMo performance figures in the README are Activeloop-reported results for its described setup, not results reproduced here. Current retrieval, corrections, deletion, isolation, latency, cost and storage remain unknown from this source-only review.

benchmark.note: Hivemind, its tests, and benchmark workloads were not run. Source observations and upstream-reported README figures are not Hivemind benchmark results.
